deep.reconstruction:
Latin note (top of page). Riemann sets up the attraction (Newtonian potential, kernel 1/r) of an infinite elliptic cylinder. Its axis is the x-axis and its cross-section is the ellipse E: y^2/alpha^2 + z^2/beta^2 <= 1. The machine reading 'x^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2' is doubtful. The notation on the next page (y = alpha cos psi, z = beta sin psi, point (a,b,c)) shows the section lies in the (y,z) plane.

The mass is distributed antisymmetrically: density +1/2 for x>0 and -1/2 for x<0. Riemann asks for the components X, Y, Z at the point o = (a,b,c). He writes only fragments: 'X = 2 eps a pi ...' (my reading of '2 a pi'), 'Y = ∫', and 'Z ='. Here eps = 0, +1, -1 according as the point lies outside the cylinder, in its positive part, or in its negative part. The integral runs over psi from 0 to 2 pi, i.e. around the boundary ellipse. He concludes: 'Unde attractio cylindri utcumque finiti facile determinatur.'

The following steps are my reconstruction, consistent with the fragments.

(1) Set d^2 = (y-b)^2 + (z-c)^2 and R = sqrt(a^2 + d^2). Integrate the kernel over x:
- int_0^oo (x-a) dx/((x-a)^2+d^2)^(3/2) = 1/R.
- int_{-oo}^0 (x-a) dx/((x-a)^2+d^2)^(3/2) = -1/R.
With densities +1/2 and -1/2 this gives X = ∫∫_E dy dz / sqrt(a^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2). This is the potential, at height a, of the elliptic lamina E.

(2) Use polar coordinates (rho, theta) about the foot (b,c): ∫_0^rho r dr/sqrt(a^2+r^2) = sqrt(a^2+rho^2) - |a|.
- If (b,c) lies inside E, the full turn of theta contributes -2 pi |a| = -2 pi eps a. If it lies outside, these terms cancel.
- The remainder is a line integral over the boundary point (alpha cos psi, beta sin psi). It involves the distance sqrt(a^2+(alpha cos psi - b)^2 + (beta sin psi - c)^2).
So X = (boundary integral over psi from 0 to 2 pi) - 2 pi eps a, up to sign convention. This matches the '2 eps a pi' plus psi-integral structure.

(3) For Y: int_0^oo dx/((x-a)^2+d^2)^(3/2) = (1+a/R)/d^2 and int_{-oo}^0 = (1-a/R)/d^2. The antisymmetric density therefore gives Y = a ∫∫_E (y-b) dy dz/(d^2 R). Z is analogous with (z-c). In polar form Y = a ∫ cos(theta) asinh(rho(theta)/|a|) d theta, which can again be written as a psi-integral over the boundary. Riemann left Y and Z unwritten.

(4) 'Finite cylinder'. A semi-infinite cylinder x>0 of density 1 equals the infinite cylinder of density 1/2 plus the antisymmetric (+-1/2) distribution. The infinite cylinder's attraction is the classical two-dimensional one. A cylinder a1 < x < a2 is the difference of two shifted semi-infinite cylinders. Hence the finite case follows by superposition.

The next page carries this out. It reduces the distance squared a^2+(alpha cos psi-b)^2+(beta sin psi-c)^2 to a product of complex-conjugate linear factors in cos psi and sin psi. This uses the root lambda of 1 = a^2/lambda + b^2/(lambda+alpha^2) + c^2/(lambda+beta^2), i.e. ellipsoidal/confocal coordinates, aiming at elliptic integrals.

German part (lower page). These are several crossed-out drafts of a letter to a colleague ('Hochverehrter Herr College!'). Riemann returns the treatise of 'Herrn stud. Geiler' (name uncertain) with his notes and remarks. He asks the colleague to pass the remarks to the student when the treatise is returned, so the author can see what changes are needed. There is no mathematics in this part. Context from the previous page: Pisa, late 1863.
errors: The formulas are only fragments ('X = 2 a pi ...', 'Y = ∫', 'Z ='), so the sign and normalisation of the -2 pi eps a term cannot be checked against Riemann's own final expression.

The machine transcription's 'x^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2' clashes with using the point o(a,b,c) and with the next page's y = alpha cos psi, z = beta sin psi. The section is almost certainly y^2/alpha^2 + z^2/beta^2 <= 1. Either Riemann reused letters or the transcription misreads Greek letters.

results.what: Attraction of an antisymmetrically loaded (+-1/2) infinite elliptic cylinder reduced, by integrating along the axis, to the potential of an elliptic lamina, then to a boundary integral over psi with a jump term 2 pi eps a (eps = 0, +-1 by location of the point).
results.modern_name: Newtonian potential of a cylinder/lamina; reduction of an area integral to a boundary line integral (solid-angle style jump term)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical potential theory (Laplace, Gauss, Dirichlet, 19th-century attraction literature)

results.what: Attraction of a finite (arbitrarily bounded) cylinder by superposing semi-infinite cylinders, each split into a uniform infinite cylinder plus an antisymmetric part.
Letter drafts returning a student's treatise (stud. Geiler?) with referee-type remarks.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine potential-theory computation (attraction of a cylinder via an antisymmetric density and boundary integrals), only sketched. The rest of the page is letter drafts. Nothing here goes beyond the known 19th-century attraction literature.

checkable.asserts: x-integral of the axial kernel over x>0 equals 1/R (should give 0)
x-integral over x<0 equals -1/R, so the +-1/2 density yields X = ∫∫ dy dz/R (should give 0)
transverse kernel after x-integration with antisymmetric density is a/(d^2 R) (should give 0)
radial integral giving the boundary term minus |a|, the source of the 2 pi eps a jump (should give 0)

transcription_corrections: First line: probably 'y^2/alpha^2 + z^2/beta^2 <= 1' (cross-section in the y,z plane), not 'x^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2'.
'X = 2 alpha pi' is more plausibly 'X = 2 eps a pi ...' (the eps defined just below).
'densitate [?] pro valoribus negativis' should be 'densitate -1/2 pro valoribus negativis ipsius x'.
The heading 'Bemerkungen zu der Abhandlung des Herrn Geiler' and the name 'stud. Geiler' are uncertain readings; likewise 'Kirchhoff's Zeitung' and 'Herrn Ende' are doubtful.
